title: 門の前のメロディー  (The Tune at the Gate)

segments.t: Mio hurries to the open courtyard gate with Takashi and Kazuko, calling warmly to the older neighbour who stood listening on Keyaki Lane. Listen first.
すみません、よろしければ中に入って、温かいお茶を一杯いかがですか？
待ってください……十番地のバイオリン工房のお隣さんじゃありませんか！？
お知り合いなんですか、隆さん！？
三十年前、毎週金曜日の六時にバイオリンを持ってここへ来てくださっていたんです！
待って……古いハガキを見てください！「パン屋さんと先生に、隅の椅子を二つ取っておいてください」！
隆さんの叔母様と金曜日の二重奏を弾いていた、音楽の先生だったんですね！
誰がついに五月のワルツの後半を仕上げたのかと、今聞かれましたよ！
窓から私の十六小節が聞こえたとき、何とおっしゃいましたか、隆さん？
目に涙を浮かべて、まるで叔母の声そのものだったと言っていました！
今週の金曜日、六時のグランドオープンにお誘いしましたか！？
バイオリンを持って来ると約束してくれました……しかも通りの近所の人を十人も一緒に！
近所の人が十人も！？金曜日までに、由香さんのレモンが二倍いりますね！
Now let's go through it line by line with the English translation.
すみません、よろしければ中に入って、温かいお茶を一杯いかがですか？
'Excuse me, sir—would you like to come inside for a warm cup of tea?' "Ikaga desu ka" is the graceful, welcoming cousin of 'how about it?', ideal whenever you offer a guest tea at the door.
待ってください……十番地のバイオリン工房のお隣さんじゃありませんか！？

'Wait... aren't you our neighbour from the violin shop at number ten?!' Wrapping 'next door' in polite "o-" at the front and "-san" at the back creates the warm Japanese word for a cherished neighbour.
お知り合いなんですか、隆さん！？
'You know each other, Takashi?!' Built from 'know each other', "oshiriai" is a polite, gentle word for an acquaintance or old friend.
三十年前、毎週金曜日の六時にバイオリンを持ってここへ来てくださっていたんです！
'Thirty years ago, he brought his violin here every Friday at six!' Adding "kudasatte ita" onto 'came' folds gratitude right into the memory—saying he kindly came week after week.
待って……古いハガキを見てください！「パン屋さんと先生に、隅の椅子を二つ取っておいてください」！
'Wait—look at our old postcard: "Save two corner chairs for the baker and the teacher"!' Joining 'take' with "oku" means setting something aside in advance—saving those two chairs for Friday evening.
隆さんの叔母様と金曜日の二重奏を弾いていた、音楽の先生だったんですね！
'He was the music teacher who played Friday duets with your aunt, Takashi!' The word for 'duet' stacks three kanji—'two', 'layered', and 'perform music'—two instruments weaving one song.
誰がついに五月のワルツの後半を仕上げたのかと、今聞かれましたよ！
'He just asked me who finally finished the second half of her May waltz!' Notice the word for 'at long last':
ついに。
Japanese saves this word for moments that took real waiting—like a thirty-year-old melody finally getting its ending.
窓から私の十六小節が聞こえたとき、何とおっしゃいましたか、隆さん？
'What did he say when he heard my sixteen bars through the window, Takashi?' Musical bars are counted with a compound that literally means 'small joints', like the neat nodes along a stalk of bamboo.
目に涙を浮かべて、まるで叔母の声そのものだったと言っていました！
'He had tears in his eyes—he said it sounded just like her own voice!' Japanese pictures welling up as 'floating tears in one's eyes', a quiet, poetic phrase for being deeply moved.
今週の金曜日、六時のグランドオープンにお誘いしましたか！？
'Did you invite him to our grand opening this Friday at six o'clock?!' Wrapping the stem of 'invite' in "o-sasoi shimashita" creates the respectful humble phrasing for inviting an honoured neighbour.
バイオリンを持って来ると約束してくれました……しかも通りの近所の人を十人も一緒に！
'He promised to bring his violin—and ten neighbours from down the street!' "Shikamo" means 'and on top of that!', piling one piece of happy news right onto the last.
近所の人が十人も！？金曜日までに、由香さんのレモンが二倍いりますね！
'Ten extra neighbours?! Yuka is going to need twice as many lemons by Friday!' Adding tiny "mo" right onto 'ten people' puts wide-eyed amazement in Mio's voice: 'a whole ten people?!'.
Now let's listen to the whole conversation one last time.

近所の人が十人も！？金曜日までに、由香さんのレモンが二倍いりますね！
The Friday duet partner from thirty years ago heard the open window and is bringing his violin—and half the street—back this Friday at six for the Season 2 finale! See you next time.
またね！
